observation.visible_scene: A nighttime waterfront view: a dark sky above a calm body of water, with a low city skyline (lit buildings, a bridge strung with lights, a tall lit tower near center-right) along the horizon. Fireworks detonate in the sky and their light, plus the city lights, is mirrored on the water surface below.
visible_changes: At the start a large spherical firework burst (white/green sparks mixed with pink) is already fully expanded high in the center sky and is fading; over frames 1-10 its sparks thin out and its color shifts toward pink/red as it dims, with a smoke plume lingering above it.
Around frames 11-16 one or more small bright pink flashes/crackles appear inside the residual smoke cloud left by the first burst (secondary bursts within the smoke, not a new launch position).

From about frame 22 a new bright red light emerges at the horizon line near center, growing into a persistent upward-fanning 'willow/fan' burst that stays lit and roughly constant in shape through the end of the clip (frames 24-41).
A strong vertical red reflection of that horizon fan burst appears on the water directly beneath it and tracks its brightness.
From about frame 32-35 a separate small pink burst appears higher in the sky (above and right of the fan burst) and remains visible, slowly fading, through the final frames.
The city skyline and bridge lights stay in fixed positions across all frames; only the water's reflected streaks shimmer and shift slightly.
outside_clip_unknowns: The launch or detonation that produced the first spherical burst (it is already mid-fade at frame 1).
Whether the horizon fan burst and the higher pink burst are still expanding, will fade, or are followed by more fireworks after the last frame.
The source of the small flashes within the smoke cloud.
uncertain_details: Camera appears essentially static (background buildings unchanged), but slight handheld jitter cannot be ruled out.
The bright column on the water is interpreted as a reflection of the horizon fan burst rather than a separate object; the same applies to the first burst's reflection.
It is unclear whether the horizon red light is a low-altitude explosion or a ground/water-level fan effect; only its sustained bright fan shape is visible.
The pink flashes in the smoke (frames 11-16) could be lingering embers or a second small burst; the clip does not resolve this.
